extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing YA fiction writers / novelists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and quality criteria for writing Young Adult (YA) fiction aimed at readers aged ~12–18, covering voice, themes, pacing, character development, and distinctions from adjacent age categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target readership should be adolescents roughly ages 12–18; tone, stakes, and protagonist age should align with this audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist (age & POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: usually 15–18, written from teen POV (no adult-looking-back)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonists are typically mid- to late-teens and the narrative voice should be that of a teen experiencing events in the present, not an adult narrator reflecting back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: present-tense lived experience, not retrospective wisdom
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YA tone should convey immediacy and lived experience rather than mature hindsight or moralizing; the story should feel like it's happening now to the teen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic Teen Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator must inhabit teen consciousness — vocabulary, concerns, slang, but without parodying. No "adult hindsight." The story is happening now to this teen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vocabulary and concerns consistent with teen experience; avoid imitation, caricature, or inserting adult interpretation. Voice should feel natural and credible for a teen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coming-of-Age Themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity formation; First love; Family conflict; Friendship and betrayal; Authority and rebellion; Mortality (often confronted for the first time); Sexual awakening; Mental health
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theme areas are central to YA and should be treated as formative experiences shaping the protagonist's growth. A YA work may center one or several of these themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated Internal + External Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: External conflicts (school, family, antagonists) directly mirror/trigger internal struggles (identity, self-worth, belonging). Quality YA weaves them inseparably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot-level (external) stakes should be tied to the character's inner life; conflicts should serve both narrative momentum and emotional/psychological development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing & Compelling Story
rubrics_metrics.description: "YA readers are some of your toughest readers." Story momentum matters; baggy MFA-style work doesn't fly. Sentence-level mastery less critical than narrative engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot propulsion and clear narrative drive. While prose craft matters, YA often rewards a fast-moving, engaging narrative over ornate sentence-level experimentation that slows momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopeful Endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Not necessarily happy — but the journey must imply possibility. Most YA closes on a hopeful note showing the character has grown and will survive. (This distinguishes YA from "literary adult" which may end in despair.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings should leave room for growth or survival; avoid bleak finality. The resolution should suggest the protagonist has acquired resources or insight to go on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal growth is the spine. The character at the end has learned, changed, become more themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth should be central and evident; the arc must show measurable internal change tied to events of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenres (as production categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary YA; YA Fantasy; YA Sci-fi/Dystopia; YA Romance; YA Thriller / Horror; YA Issue Books; Verse novels
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these subgenre distinctions to calibrate conventions, stakes, tone, and content expectations (e.g., romance vs. dystopia vs. issue-driven narratives). Examples/authors listed for orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Narrator's Age Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quick check to ensure voice authenticity — language, perspective, and concerns should read like a teen rather than an older person's reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Appropriate Stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Are stakes appropriate to teen life (not trivialized, not over-amplified)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakes should be meaningful within the teen's world; avoid diminishing teen problems as petty or overstating consequences beyond plausible teen experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Protagonist Drives Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the protagonist drive the plot?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure agency: the main character's decisions, desires, and flaws should be the engine of the narrative, not purely external forces or adult interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Avoid Talking Down or Moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work avoid talking down or moralizing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YA should treat adolescent experience seriously and respectfully; avoid didactic tones, sermonizing, or simplifying complex teen issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Hope Present at the End
rubrics_metrics.description: Is hope present at the end (even if hard-won)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ending should allow for possibility and resilience rather than final despair, aligning with YA's tendency toward hopeful closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Honor Adolescence as Serious Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story honor adolescence as serious life?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray teenage experiences as consequential and real; avoid minimizing adolescent feelings or experiences as merely preparatory for adulthood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison — Middle Grade (MG) vs YA
rubrics_metrics.description: MG (8–12): protagonists 8–13; clearer moral; less romance/sex
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions to set appropriate protagonist age, content level, and thematic complexity when positioning a work for MG vs YA readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison — New Adult vs YA
rubrics_metrics.description: New Adult (18–25): college/first job; explicit content allowed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If protagonist and content move into post-adolescent life and more explicit material, consider New Adult classification rather than YA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison — Adult vs YA
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult: any age protagonist; full range of content/themes/style
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adult fiction permits broader stylistic choices, mature perspectives, and content; distinguish YA by teen POV, immediacy, and coming-of-age focus.
